newsitem.title: USA: GM - strike settlement doesn't block job plans.
newsitem.headline: GM - strike settlement doesn't block job plans.

text.p: General Motors Corp. Chairman Jack Smith said Monday a parts plant strike settlement that called for the automaker to add 420 jobs does not interfere with GM's ongoing push to cut its work force through attrition.
Asked about the agreement at a Greater Detroit Chamber of Commerce lunch, Smith said: "It's the same, nothing's really new. We're comfortable where we are."

GM agreed to add the jobs, pay out more than $2 million to settle grievances and keep some wheel production at the plant until 2002. Investors responded by pushing GM's stock price up $1.75 to $58.625 a share in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.

Workers from United Auto Worker Local 909 approved the settlement and returned to work at the Warren, Mich., powertrain facility late Sunday. The plant makes transmissions, wheels and other suspension components for many of GM's North American light vehicles.
About 2,800 hourly workers walked off the job July 22 when a new contract was not reached by the midnight strike deadline.

Smith said he hoped the automaker and UAW leaders can avoid more strikes as they work on the remaining nine local agreements that are still left out of the 105 UAW locals GM deals with in the United States.
"We're still struggling to stay competitive and we'll take them one at a time," Smith said.

Locals without contracts include two Delphi Chassis System brake plants in Dayton, Ohio; a GM Powertrain plant in Ypsilanti, Mich., which makes automatic rear-wheel drive and front-wheel drive transmissions; an engine plant in Romulus, Mich.; the Cadillac assembly plant in Hamtramck, Mich.; Detroit Assembly, which makes commercial truck and recreational vehicle chassis; warehouse workers in Waterford Township, Mich.; and hourly workers at GM's Tech Centre in Warren, Mich.

GM, which is trying to shrink its work force through attrition and avoid hiring new workers, has been hit with six strikes since the beginning of 1997. In addition to Warren, the strikes included an 87-day walkout at the Pontiac, Mich., full-size pickup truck factory; a 50-day strike at the Oklahoma City, Okla., car plant; a 14-day strike by workers at the Fort Wayne, Ind., full-size pickup truck plant; and two strikes by the International Brotherhood of Electronic Workers.

Hourly workers from UAW Local 663 in Anderson, Ind., were scheduled to finish voting on a new contract Monday. The 2,500 union members work at a Delphi Interior & Lighting plant that makes tail lamps. A tentative agreement was reached early July 23, about two hours after a strike deadline passed.
Meantime, GM said Monday that it will resume production Tuesday at several car plants that had been idled because of the Warren strike.

GM said its two Oshawa, Ontario, car plants will re-start production on the first shift Tuesday. Production at two Michigan car assembly plants, the Buick City facility in Flint, the Orion Township plant, will re-start production with the second shift Tuesday.

The four facilities were part of the six plants and 16,500 workers that GM idled in response to the transmission strike. Two remaining facilities in Lansing, Mich., are expected to resume operations sometime Wednesday, said GM spokesman Tom Klipstine.
